rules.message: A `setX(...)` state setter call appears LEXICALLY AFTER an async boundary (an `await`, or a `.then(`/`.catch(`/`.finally(` continuation) in the same function body, with no unmount/abort guard (`AbortController`/`AbortSignal`/`isMounted`/`mountedRef`/`signal:`/`cancelled`/`didCancel`) anywhere in that body — the reported line is the first setter that actually follows the boundary, not merely one that shares the function with it. "Same function" means the NEAREST enclosing function, not the whole declaration: a boundary in a sibling closure no longer qualifies (measured on a 22-tree corpus: 6 of 87 findings changed — 4 dropped as sibling-closure or nested-callback pairings, 2 re-anchored onto a setter that genuinely follows a boundary in its own function), while a `.then(`/`.catch(`/`.finally(` continuation callback is scoped together with the call that schedules it, so a continuation setting state still fires. The flip side of that scoping: a setter inside a NESTED callback (a `.map`/`forEach`/`setTimeout`/event-handler closure) whose only boundary sits outside that callback no longer fires — an accepted under-report. The narrowing needs parser-projected function spans; a file whose spans could not be projected (parse failure, size cap, an external-parser envelope that omits them) keeps the old whole-declaration scope and its sibling-closure false positives. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. This is a TEXTUAL ORDER claim, not a dataflow one: it does not prove the setter runs on the resumed continuation (a setter in an `else` branch still counts, and so does one that follows a CONDITIONAL boundary — `if (stale) { await refresh(); }` then `setX(...)` fires even on the path where nothing was awaited), and it does NOT prove the component can unmount while the request is in flight (a plain event handler is mounted by construction whenever it fires, so a `setX(...)` inside one is an accepted false positive here). SAME-LINE NESTING RESIDUAL (a MEASURED false negative, disclosed rather than fixed): on a single line "after" is decided by MATCH START OFFSET, so an `await` nested INSIDE the setter call's own argument list reads as coming AFTER it and does not pair — `setData(await fetch(url));` is silently NOT reported, while the two-statement spelling (`const r = await fetch(url); setData(r);`) fires, same file, same run. This is the mirror image of the `p.then(r => setX(r))` one-liner that DOES fire (there the boundary token starts first); closing it would need structural nesting awareness that a start-offset comparison between two independent regexes cannot have. But when the setter genuinely follows an in-flight await inside code that CAN unmount mid-request (an effect's async loader, a callback stored across a lifecycle boundary), the resolve races teardown: the classic "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component" warning, a stale-data flash overwriting newer state, or a wasted render right after remount. Thread an `AbortController` (or an `isMounted`/`mountedRef` flag) through the async function and skip the `setX(...)` call if the request was aborted or the component has unmounted. The `require_file` gate scopes this to React files (a `useEffect`/`useState` call, or a `from 'react'` import) to keep it out of non-component async helpers. The `setX(` trigger is anchored to a bare (non-member) call so a `localStorage.setItem`/`res.setHeader`/`date.setHours` is not mistaken for a state setter, and `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`setImmediate` are vetoed — so a genuine `setX(...)` that merely coexists with a timer in the same function is an accepted under-report. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-setstate-after-async-unguarded-ok`.
